script.opening: “Hello doctor. Yes, I can see you. The nurse said you wanted to talk about my weight. I’m just tired, really. Old age. And the flat’s a bit cold these days, that’s all.”

facts.text: If asked: “Sunny’s at work till six. It’s just me.” If asked to show the room on camera, he turns the tablet round: an empty living room, a coat on the chair. He is wearing a coat and hat indoors.

“I don’t eat much. Toast, tea, some soup.” If asked why: “There’s not much in. Sunny does the shopping.” If asked about money for food: “He gives me ten pounds a week. It’s enough for bread and milk.” Lost weight “since the summer”.

If asked: no cough, no blood in the phlegm, no difficulty swallowing, no tummy pain, bowels normal, no blood in the stools, no night sweats, passing water normally. Not more thirsty. Feels cold and tired.
“Sunny says the heating costs too much, so it goes on for an hour at night.” The flat is his own; he bought it with his late wife Kamaljit.

Only if asked who manages his money: “Sunny has my bank card since the stroke, to help with shopping. He knows my number.” If asked further: “He borrowed twelve thousand pounds for his business. He said he would pay it back. It was our savings, mine and Kamaljit’s.” He has signed “some papers from the bank — I didn’t read them, my eyes”.
If asked: “Sometimes the tablets run out and Sunny forgets to collect them.” Has missed his blood pressure and cholesterol tablets “for a week or two at a time”.
If asked: “I feel useless. A burden.” Sleeps poorly because of the cold. If asked directly about thoughts of ending his life: “No. I have my gurdwara. Waheguru decides.”

No memory problems: he knows the date, his medicines, his bank, and follows everything the doctor says. Used to be a bus driver for 30 years; reads Punjabi and English but small print is hard (needs new glasses).

Wife died 2022. Daughter Harpreet lives in Canada; they speak on WhatsApp on Sundays. “I don’t want to worry her.” Sunny is his late sister’s son, 38. Friends at the gurdwara “ask why I don’t come any more — I can’t pay for the taxi”.

Only if asked whether Sunny has ever hurt him, frightened him or whether he feels safe: pause, then “Last week I asked for my card back. He shouted and grabbed my arm. Here.” (Shows a small yellow bruise on the forearm.) “He said if I make trouble he will tell the doctors I can’t cope and they’ll put me in a home.”

Dignified, polite, ashamed. Do not volunteer the money: minimise (“it’s fine, he helps me”). Open up gradually if the doctor is patient, non-judgemental and asks open questions about who helps with shopping and money. If the doctor says “this is abuse” bluntly or talks about the police straight away, become defensive: “He’s family. I don’t want him in trouble.” If the doctor explains what support could look like and that he stays in control, say: “If it is quiet… if it doesn’t shame the family… maybe.” Agree to a referral and bank contact if the doctor explains them clearly; ask that Sunny is not told it came from him.

ice.ideas: “I’m old and tired. Maybe I need vitamins.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Sunny shouted at him and grabbed his arm when he asked for his bank card, and threatened that “they’ll put you in a home” if he makes trouble. He is frightened of losing his flat and independence and of shaming the family. He shares this only if asked kindly and directly whether he feels safe or whether anyone has hurt or frightened him.
ice.expectations: “Some tablets for tiredness.” Underneath: help to get control of his money back without his nephew being punished or the family finding out.

cues: Wearing a coat and hat indoors; “the flat’s a bit cold these days” — heating restricted.
“There’s not much in. Sunny does the shopping.” — dependence and possible neglect.
“He said he would pay it back. It was our savings.” — a large transfer he regrets; possible financial abuse.

checkpoints.text: Checks he is alone and can talk privately on the video (asks him to show the room or confirms no one can overhear), and agrees what to do if someone comes in

Explores the weight loss and tiredness, including a screen for other causes (cancer red flags, diabetes, thyroid, mood), and arranges proportionate tests — while noticing the coat indoors, little food and restricted heating
Asks open, non-judgemental questions about who manages his shopping, money and medicines, and uncovers the bank card, £10 a week, the £12,000 and the unread papers
Asks directly but gently whether he feels safe and whether anyone has hurt, threatened or frightened him — and finds the arm-grab, bruise and threat
Recognises possible financial abuse, neglect and physical abuse of an adult with care and support needs, and explains safeguarding under the Care Act 2014 in plain terms

Assesses his capacity for the decision about a referral (understands, retains, weighs, communicates), respects his choice, and explains honestly when information may be shared without consent (serious risk, others at risk, a crime, coercion)

Agrees a concrete plan: safeguarding referral to adult social care with consent; contacting his bank (card, PIN, safeguarding team); restarting medicines via pharmacy delivery; bloods; safe contact arrangements; signposting (Age UK, police if he wishes); follow-up within a week; documents carefully
Responds to shame and family loyalty with dignity and respect, keeps him in control of decisions, and avoids blaming language about his nephew

worked.txt: “Before we start, is anyone else at home, or could anyone overhear? … Thank you. If someone comes in, just say ‘can we talk about my tablets’ and I’ll know.”
“Since the stroke, who helps you with the shopping and with money? … How does that work day to day?”
“I can see you’re wearing your coat indoors, and you’ve told me there’s not much food in and the heating’s only on for an hour. That worries me — it’s affecting your health.”
“Some people in your situation feel frightened or are treated roughly by someone close to them. Has anyone hurt you, threatened you or made you feel afraid?”

“What you’re describing — someone controlling your money so you can’t buy food or heat your flat, and grabbing you — is something the council’s adult safeguarding team can help with. It isn’t about punishing Sunny. It’s about you being safe and in charge of your own money. You stay part of every decision.”

“I won’t do anything behind your back. The only time I’d have to share this without your agreement is if I thought you or someone else were at serious risk, or a serious crime — and even then I’d tell you first if I could.”

f.learning: Financial abuse of older people often presents as a health problem — weight loss, cold, missed medicines, missed appointments — with a relative who answers for the patient. See the person alone (on video, check the room), ask open questions about who manages money and shopping, and ask directly about safety. Under the Care Act 2014 an adult with care and support needs who is experiencing, or at risk of, abuse or neglect and cannot protect himself because of those needs should be considered for a safeguarding enquiry. A person with capacity has the right to make decisions about his own life; seek consent for a referral, explain what will happen, and know the exceptions (risk to others, serious crime, coercion or undue influence, vital interests). Treat the health effects too, and follow up soon.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: Care Act 2014 (section 42 safeguarding enquiries) and Care and support statutory guidance (DHSC) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 and Code of Practice (2007) · GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information (2017) · GMC Good medical practice (2024) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, updated 2026) · Office of the Public Guardian guidance on reporting concerns about an attorney or deputy
knowledge.summary: Weight loss, cold and missed medicines with a relative controlling the money: see him alone, ask about safety, assess capacity and seek consent for a safeguarding referral.

points.t: Signs include unexplained loss of savings, someone else controlling bank cards or PINs, lack of food or heating despite adequate income, unpaid bills, new “loans” to relatives, signing documents not understood, and isolation from friends.

Physical injury or threats, fear of the carer, being prevented from seeing professionals, coercion over legal documents, or risk to others in the household — these raise urgency and may justify sharing without consent.

Do not assume all weight loss is from lack of food. Screen for cancer red flags (NICE NG12 includes unexplained weight loss), diabetes, thyroid disease and depression. Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, HbA1c, TSH, CRP, ferritin; consider other tests by symptoms.

The local authority must make enquiries where an adult has care and support needs, is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect (including financial abuse), and as a result of those needs cannot protect themselves. Making Safeguarding Personal: ask the person what outcome they want.

Presume capacity (MCA 2005). If he can understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision about referral, his choice is respected. Share without consent if others are at risk, a serious crime is involved, there is coercion or undue influence, or to protect vital interests — and document the reasoning.

With consent: contact his bank (cancel and reissue the card, new PIN, bank safeguarding team), check whether any power of attorney exists (Office of the Public Guardian if an attorney is misusing it), pharmacy delivery and a medicines compliance check, benefits and heating support, Age UK. Police if theft or assault and he wishes to report — or if risk is serious.
Agree how to contact him safely (times when he is alone, a code phrase), book follow-up within a week, and document carefully in his own words without making the record visible to others with access.
If he is hurt or threatened, or feels unsafe at home — 999. If he is prevented from attending or contacting the surgery, the practice will follow up.

model.text: Hello Mr Bhatti, I’m Dr Lee. Thank you for joining. Before we start — is anyone else at home, or could anyone overhear us?
model.why: Checks privacy before a sensitive conversation

model.text: No, Sunny’s at work till six. It’s just me.
Thank you. The nurse mentioned you’ve lost some weight. How have you been feeling?
Just tired, doctor. Old age. And the flat’s a bit cold these days.
I notice you’re wearing your coat and hat indoors. Tell me about the cold, and about food — what have you been eating?
model.why: Responds to a visual cue without judgement

model.text: Sunny says the heating costs too much — an hour at night. Toast, soup. There’s not much in.
Have you had any cough, trouble swallowing, tummy pain, change in your bowels, blood anywhere, or sweats at night?
model.why: Screens for other causes of weight loss

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Since your stroke, who helps you with shopping and money? How does that work?
Sunny has my card. He gives me ten pounds a week. He borrowed twelve thousand for his business… it was our savings. He’ll pay it back.
Thank you for trusting me with that. Can I ask — has Sunny, or anyone, ever hurt you, threatened you or made you feel afraid?
Last week I asked for my card back. He shouted, grabbed my arm. Said if I make trouble the doctors will put me in a home.
I’m really sorry that happened. Nobody is going to put you in a home for asking for your own money — you’re clearly able to make your own decisions. What would you like to happen?
model.why: Reassures, affirms capacity and asks for his desired outcome

model.text: I want my card back. But he’s my sister’s son. I don’t want him in trouble, or the family to know.

That makes sense. There’s a team at the council — adult safeguarding — whose job is to help people in exactly this situation get control back and stay safe. It’s not about punishing Sunny. With your permission I’d refer you to them, and they’d talk to you about what you want. Would that be all right?
If it is quiet. If they don’t say it came from me.

I’ll ask them to be careful about that and to contact you when you’re alone. I also want to be honest: if I thought you were in serious danger, I might need to share information even if you didn’t want me to — and I’d tell you first if I could. Can I also help you call your bank today to stop the card and get a new PIN?
model.why: Honest about the limits of confidentiality; practical protection

model.text: Yes. That would help.

For your health: I’ll ask the chemist to deliver your tablets so they don’t run out, and I’d like some blood tests this week. I’ll also ask about help with heating costs. When is a safe time for us to phone you?
model.why: Treats health effects and agrees safe contact

model.text: Mornings, before ten. He sleeps.
Then we’ll call mornings. If he hurts or threatens you again, or you feel unsafe, call 999. I’ll call you within a week. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
Council safeguarding, the bank, tablets delivered, blood test, you ring in the morning.
That’s right. You’ve been very brave today, Mr Bhatti.

social.t: Many older people do not report abuse by relatives because of love, dependence, fear of losing their home and community shame. Respect this; focus on the outcome he wants.
Stopped attending the gurdwara because of money for taxis; reconnecting with his community and daughter is protective.
Cold homes worsen cardiovascular and respiratory health in older people; benefits checks and warm-home schemes help.

legal.t: Section 42 duty for the local authority to make safeguarding enquiries. Six principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, accountability.
Capacity is decision-specific and presumed. An unwise decision is not proof of incapacity.

If someone is acting under a lasting power of attorney and misusing it, the Office of the Public Guardian can investigate. Taking money without consent can be theft or fraud by abuse of position (Fraud Act 2006).

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): share without consent where necessary to protect others, prevent serious crime, or where the adult’s decision may be under coercion or undue influence; tell the patient where safe and document the reasons.
Record exactly what he said, the bruise seen on video, capacity assessment, consent and actions — and consider record-access controls if the nephew has proxy access.

community.t: Age UK advice line, Hourglass (safer ageing) helpline, Action Fraud for financial crime, bank safeguarding teams, local warm-home and benefits services, gurdwara community support.

redFlags: Injury, threats or fear of the carer
Large unexplained financial losses or documents signed under pressure
Being prevented from accessing care or professionals
Cancer red flags with weight loss (dysphagia, haemoptysis, bleeding, night sweats)
psychosocial: Nephew controls card and PIN; £10 a week for food; heating restricted
Shame and family loyalty; fear of a care home
ice: Concern: nephew in trouble, family shame, being put in a home
Expectation: tablets for tiredness; underneath, control of his money back

playbook.diagnosis: Possible financial abuse with neglect and an episode of physical abuse in a 79-year-old with care and support needs after a stroke, with weight loss and missed medication; other causes of weight loss still to be excluded.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Some of what’s making you tired and thin is not having enough food or heat, because you don’t have control of your own money. That’s not right, and there is help to change it.”

management.reflectIce: “You don’t want Sunny punished, and you want your card back. Let’s aim for exactly that.”
management.psychosocial: Seen alone; capacity assessed; safe contact times agreed; community reconnection.
sharedPlan: Safeguarding referral to adult social care with consent; ask for discreet contact
Call the bank together: stop card, new PIN, safeguarding team
Pharmacy delivery and compliance check; restart medicines
Bloods this week for weight loss; review BP
Benefits and warm-home referral; Age UK
safetyNet: 999 if hurt or threatened or feels unsafe
GP call within a week, mornings before ten

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by staying on the medical model (“bloods for tiredness”) and never asking about money or safety — or by over-riding a capable man’s wishes.

items.fail: Never checking that he is alone on the video.
items.why: He cannot disclose if the nephew might overhear.
items.fix: Ask who is there and, if needed, to show the room.

items.fail: Ordering bloods for tiredness and ending there.
items.why: Misses the coat indoors, the food and heating, and the abuse.
items.fix: Ask who manages his money and shopping.

items.fail: Calling the police or referring without discussing it with him.
items.why: He has capacity and wants a say; acting over him without a legal basis damages trust.

items.fail: Doing nothing because “he doesn’t want a fuss”.
items.why: There is assault and ongoing financial harm; safeguarding duties apply.
items.fix: Explore what support he would accept and agree concrete steps.

items.fail: Using blaming language about the nephew.
items.why: Provokes family loyalty and shuts down the conversation.
items.fix: Focus on his safety and control, not on punishing Sunny.

items.why: Contact at the wrong time could alert the nephew and increase risk.
items.fix: Agree safe times and a code phrase.

wordPics.clearFail: Treats as tiredness only; never asks about money or safety; or refers to police without his knowledge; no follow-up.
wordPics.fail: Picks up some cues but does not explore safety, does not explain safeguarding, or ignores his wishes; vague plan.
wordPics.pass: Checks privacy, uncovers the financial control, asks about safety, explains safeguarding, seeks consent for referral and arranges follow-up.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: screens weight loss properly, assesses capacity explicitly, is honest about confidentiality limits, agrees practical steps (bank, pharmacy, heating), arranges safe contact and keeps his dignity and choices central.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: screens weight loss properly, assesses capacity explicitly, is honest about confidentiality limits, agrees practical steps (bank, pharmacy, heating), arranges safe contact and keeps his dignity and choices central.

avoid.dont: “Your nephew is stealing from you — that’s abuse.”
avoid.instead: “Someone controlling your money so you can’t buy food or heat your home isn’t right, and there is help.”
avoid.why: Blaming language provokes loyalty and shame.

avoid.dont: “I have to report this to the police.”
avoid.instead: “With your permission I’d like to refer you to the council’s safeguarding team — you stay part of every decision.”
avoid.why: He has capacity; consent and choice come first unless an exception applies.

avoid.dont: “Let’s do some bloods for your tiredness.” (and stop there)
avoid.instead: “I’ll check your bloods — and I’d also like to understand who helps you with shopping and money.”
avoid.why: The medical model alone misses the abuse.
